problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Colonies of small sap-sucking insects on new shoots and the undersides of leaves.
prevention: Natural predators such as ladybugs often keep aphids down

problems.name: Corn earworm and other caterpillars
problems.signs: Caterpillars ('worms') feeding on the plants and pods; the Georgia guide calls corn earworm the most common.

problems.name: Root-knot nematodes
problems.signs: Stunted, yellow or poorly producing plants; roots show galls and swellings when pulled up.
prevention: Do not follow nematode-susceptible crops such as tomato or sweet potato
Soil solarization reduces problems in a garden bed
Cover crops can help suppress nematodes

problems.name: Fusarium and Verticillium wilt
problems.signs: Yellowing, stunting and persistent wilt even when the soil is moist; no cure once infected.

problems.name: Stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs
problems.signs: Misshapen, twisted or distorted pods, sometimes with pale or corky feeding spots.
prevention: Check pods, stems and leaf undersides for adults, nymphs and egg clusters

problems.name: Damping off and root rot
problems.signs: Young seedlings rot and die; root decay is more common when okra is planted in cold, wet soil.
prevention: Wait until the soil is warm before sowing

problems.name: Southern blight
problems.signs: Attacks the base of the plant and destroys the tissue; the fungus stays in the soil from one year to the next.
prevention: Remove plants you suspect have it

problems.name: Tough, fibrous pods
problems.signs: Pods turn tough, stringy and woody when left on the plant too long, and cropping slows.
prevention: Pick every day or two while pods are small and tender

text.summary: Okra is a tall, upright, warm-season vegetable grown for its tender green or red pods. It wants full sun, warm soil and frost-free weather, and it grows fast once settled. Pods must be picked young and often to keep the plant cropping. It suits garden beds and, with a compact variety, a large pot.
text.how_to_plant: Sow okra only once frost has gone and the soil about 10 cm down has warmed to at least 18 degrees C; cooler soil risks seedlings rotting. Pick a sunny site. Soak the hard-coated seed overnight, then push it 1 to 2.5 cm into the soil. When seedlings are about 8 cm tall, thin them to between 23 and 60 cm apart, with rows at least 90 cm apart. For an early start, raise seedlings in pots indoors for three to five weeks first.
text.how_to_care: Okra likes full sun and warm weather. It copes with dry spells fairly well but crops better with a deep watering about once a week, more often in sandy soil. Keep water steady while it flowers and sets pods, keep it off the leaves, and avoid waterlogged or poorly drained soil. Mulch 5 to 8 cm deep with organic material to hold moisture and hold weeds down. Feed with a balanced fertiliser at planting, following the label, and go easy on nitrogen, which grows leaves instead of pods. Rotate where you grow it each year.
text.harvest: Allow about 50 to 70 days from sowing in warm weather, and longer where it is cool. Cut pods while they are tender, around 5 to 10 cm long; bigger pods turn tough and fibrous. Pick every day or two, and remove any old pods you missed, because they slow further cropping. The short hairs on the plant can irritate skin, so wear gloves and long sleeves. Fresh pods keep only a few days in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Sowing into cold soil, which leaves seed slow to come up and seedlings liable to rot.
Leaving pods on the plant until they are large; they turn tough and woody and slow further cropping.
Giving too much nitrogen, which makes leafy plants with poor yield.
Growing okra again where nematode-susceptible crops grew, without rotating.
Poor drainage in beds or pots, which damages the plants.
